description: We are space Glitchers, a dedicated team from Egypt participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge for the 2026-2027 edition, our mission is to build an efficient software to monitor Astronauts 'health. we are a group of ambitious people who are excited to innovate solutions, code systems, and solve space challenges using NASA data and tech.
summary:
Our project aims to enhance fire safety in space by making NASA’s microgravity combustion research easier to use and understand. We developed a web dashboard that consolidates key research information in one place. The dashboard focuses on NASA's experiments and helps users explore their objectives, conditions, and results.
The dashboard is designed to help researchers compare experiments, identify key findings, and understand how factors such as oxygen concentration and airflow affect fire behavior in space. Our project also aims to use AI effectively to analyze available content and provide useful scientific insights. The project is important because understanding how fires behave in microgravity helps scientists improve fire prevention systems, deepen understanding of the combustion process, and suppress fires in future space missions to Mars and the Moon.

LFAEA—Scientific Information Organization, Research Summarization, Data Classification, and Analytical Methodology

1. Scientific Information Summarization

The Lunar Fire & Aerosol Evidence Atlas (LFAEA) uses a structured research-summarization approach to transform scientific publications, experimental reports, NASA investigation records, and uploaded datasets into organized and accessible scientific information.

Instead of presenting users with long technical documents and unstructured experimental files, the platform organizes the available evidence into concise investigation profiles.

Each investigation profile is divided into several information layers.

1.1 Investigation Overview

Each investigation begins with a concise scientific summary explaining:

  • The primary research objective.
  • The combustion phenomenon being investigated.
  • The experimental environment.
  • The main scientific variables.
  • The relevance of the investigation to spacecraft and lunar-habitat fire safety.

The summary is intended to communicate the purpose and scientific context of an investigation without replacing its original publication or technical report.

1.2 Scientific Significance

A separate section explains why the investigation is relevant to the overall research objectives of LFAEA.

For example, an investigation examining solid-material flame spread may be relevant to spacecraft material selection, while an investigation examining smoke aerosols may contribute to understanding smoke detection and particle transport.

Scientific relevance is therefore evaluated according to the research question rather than treating every investigation as equally useful for every application.

1.3 Experimental Variables

The platform extracts and organizes the available experimental conditions, including:

  • Gravity environment.
  • Pressure.
  • Oxygen concentration.
  • Fuel or material composition.
  • Sample geometry.
  • Airflow velocity and direction.
  • Heating conditions.
  • Experimental configuration.

These variables provide the contextual information required to interpret experimental observations.

1.4 Measurements and Experimental Endpoints

The platform separately identifies the measurements and outcomes reported by each investigation.

Depending on the experiment, these may include:

  • Flame growth and spread.
  • Flame extinction.
  • Ignition observations.
  • Smoke-point measurements.
  • Luminous flame length.
  • Aerosol particle-size distributions.
  • Temperature measurements.
  • Sensor time-series data.
  • Chemiluminescence and optical measurements.

This separation prevents experimental conditions from being confused with actual measured outcomes.

1.5 Limitations and Evidence Notes

Every investigation profile includes its important scientific limitations.

These may involve incomplete datasets, missing calibration documents, differences between experimental configurations, unresolved metadata, or limitations in transferring experimental results to lunar environments.

The platform also maintains documented facts, audit notes, and links to the associated scientific references.

2. Scientific Data Classification and Organization

LFAEA organizes investigations using multiple classification dimensions rather than assigning each experiment to a single broad category.

This allows the same investigation to appear in different research contexts depending on the user's objectives.

2.1 Research Scenario Classification

The platform currently defines six major research scenarios.

1. Lunar Habitat

Focuses on evidence relevant to combustion behavior and material safety in pressurized lunar habitats.

2. Material Flammability

Organizes investigations addressing material ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction.

3. Smoke Detection

Focuses on smoke aerosol generation, particle transport, sensing technologies, and detector-relevant measurements.

4. Suppression Research

Groups experiment with relevant to flame extinction, suppressant gases, and combustion suppression mechanisms.

5. Predictive Modelling

Identifies datasets and experimental results that may support combustion-model development, parameter studies, and model validation.

6. Crewed Habitat

Focuses on the integrated relevance of combustion research to spacecraft, orbital stations, lunar bases, and pressurized exploration vehicles.

These six scenarios form the main application-oriented classification layer.

2.2 Experimental Family Classification

Each investigation is also assigned an experimental family according to its primary subject.

The current classification includes:

Experimental family

Research focus

Gaseous Flame

Gaseous diffusion flames and cool-flame behavior

Solid Fuel

Solid-material ignition, burning, and flame spread

Liquid Droplet

Droplet combustion and extinction

Aerosol Diagnostics

Smoke particles, aerosol properties, and sensing

Solid and Gaseous Fuel

Investigations involving multiple fuel or combustion configurations

Vehicle-Scale Fire

Large-scale spacecraft fire investigations

This classification supports browsing, filtering, and identifying investigations with related scientific objectives.

2.3 Evidence Grade Classification

The investigation catalogue also assigns evidence grades from A to D.

Each record retains its grade alongside its supporting sources and limitations.

The grade is used as one component of the platform's research-priority calculation.

It must not be confused with a NASA certification, a probability of fire, or a quantitative safety rating.

2.4 Data Availability Classification

The platform distinguishes between different levels of research material availability.

The existing interface identifies records using statuses such as

  • Record: An associated investigation or source record is available.
  • Partial: Only part of the relevant documentation or data is available.
  • Pending: Additional source acquisition or verification is required.
  • External: Information is available through an external research or program page rather than the supplied dataset package.
  • Conflict: An unresolved identification or metadata discrepancy exists.

This classification helps users distinguish between documented investigations and experiments for which complete numerical analysis is not possible.

3. Investigation-Level Evidence Structure

Every investigation is represented through a standardized information structure.

The data model includes:

This structure makes different investigations easier to search, compare, and interpret using a common information framework.

4. Research Prioritization and Relevance Analysis

The platform includes a scenario-based prioritization mechanism that ranks investigations according to their relevance to the selected research scenario.

The current implementation uses a weighted heuristic score.

The scoring equation is:

Score = (0.60 × Scenario Relevance) + (0.20 × Evidence Grade) + (0.15 × Data Coverage) + (0.05 × Metadata Completeness)

The evidence-grade values used in the current implementation are

Evidence grade

Numerical value

A

100

B

78

C

66

D

35

Scenario relevance, data coverage, and metadata completeness are represented by values on a 0–100 scale in the curated investigation records.

The calculation produces a priority score out of 100.

For example, an investigation may receive a high priority in the material flammability scenario but a relatively low priority in smoke detection because its measurements are more relevant to solid-material combustion than aerosol diagnostics.

The score is recalculated when users change the selected research scenario.

Important distinction: This is a literature-navigation and research-prioritization heuristic. It is not a machine-learning prediction, fire-risk probability, or experimentally measured performance score.

5. Experimental Dataset Analysis

LFAEA includes a dedicated data-exploration component for selected experimental datasets.

The data-analysis process focuses on extracting meaningful descriptive information while preserving the original measurements and their scientific context.

The current data studio includes three principal analytical groups.

5.1 SPICE — Smoke Point Analysis

SPICE data are used to examine smoke-point outcomes under different fuel and coflow conditions.

The current platform organizes the available smoke-point records into five fuel or mixture groups:

The data are presented through an interactive bar visualization and a detailed source-level table.

The table includes:

  • Fuel or fuel mixture.
  • Number of smoke-point outcomes.
  • Burner diameter.
  • Coflow velocity.
  • Luminous flame length.

The platform also presents the empirical relationship reported in the associated peer-reviewed study:

Lsp ∝ d⁻⁰·⁹¹ ua⁰·⁴¹

Where:

  • Lsp represents luminous smoke-point flame length.
  • d represents burner diameter.
  • UA represents coflow air velocity.

The equation is retained within the limits of the studied fuels, geometries, and experimental flow conditions.

The platform explicitly distinguishes three different source-specific counts:

  • 52 smoke-point outcomes in the thesis/conference table.
  • 55 smoke points in the peer-reviewed journal paper.
  • 263 operational test points in the post-flight report.

These are different counting definitions. They must not be combined into a single total.

5.2 PSI-159 — Experimental Time-Series Analysis

The PSI-159 data section examines selected experimental sensor records and associated controller setpoint files.

Two sensor time-series datasets are included.

The platform calculates and displays descriptive statistics derived from the uploaded source columns.

These include:

  • Total sample count.
  • Recording duration.
  • Median timestamp interval.
  • Timestamp anomalies.
  • Selected channel medians.
  • Fifth and ninety-fifth percentile values.

The channel comparison includes selected source columns such as:

  • MFCA1StaticMixerFlow.
  • MFCA3FuelFlow.
  • EfieldVoltage.

The purpose is to inspect the behavior and numerical distribution of the recorded signals.

However, because the complete channel dictionary and calibration package are unavailable, the values remain source-column measurements rather than verified engineering quantities.

MFC Setpoint Analysis

The platform also organizes Mass Flow Controller setpoint records.

The selected records contain non-zero voltage values associated with experimental tests A4, C1, and H5.

These values are displayed in volts.

They are not converted into SCCM or SLPM because the required channel-specific and gas-specific calibration information is missing.

Camera Metadata Analysis

The available camera metadata are organized separately from the sensor measurements.

The uploaded records include:

  • INTNS-A4: 1,275 metadata records, with a reported frame resolution of 1392 × 1040 pixels and Mono16 pixel format.
  • ACME-H5: 286 metadata records, with a reported frame resolution of 1360 × 1024 pixels and BayerRG12 pixel format.

These are camera metadata records, not the original experimental images.

The missing TIFF/HOBJ image payloads prevent the platform from claiming that it has independently analyzed the actual flame imagery.

The analytical interface presents selected numerical ranges and available sample counts.

For Data ID 5, the current summary includes PLIF measurements and thermometry information.

For Data ID 8, the interface presents maximum-temperature ranges grouped by the available workbook condition labels.

Data ID 6 is excluded from plotting because its worksheet-column mapping is ambiguous.

Data IDs 1 and 2 retain an explicit warning because the CSV crosswalk and Excel workbook reverse the ozone descriptions.

The platform does not choose one description as correct without supporting evidence.

6. Data Processing and Analytical Workflow

The general data-processing approach consists of the following stages.

Stage 1 — Source Acquisition

Collect the available scientific publications, investigation documentation, raw data files, summary workbooks, and metadata.

Each source is registered separately and associated with its investigation where possible.

Stage 2 — Original Data Preservation

Original uploaded files are stored separately from processed information.

The raw dataset directory preserves the supplied files, while derived datasets are prepared for application use.

This separation ensures that visual processing does not overwrite or replace the original research evidence.

Stage 3 — Data Inspection

Each selected dataset is inspected to identify:

  • File structure.
  • Number of records.
  • Column names.
  • Available timestamps.
  • Measurement ranges.
  • Missing information.
  • Data-format inconsistencies.
  • Possible anomalies.

Stage 4 — Descriptive Analysis

Descriptive calculations are performed where the source data support them.

Examples include:

  • Sample counts.
  • Recording duration.
  • Median timestamp interval.
  • Median measurement values.
  • Fifth and ninety-fifth percentiles.
  • Minimum and maximum values.
  • Counts grouped by fuel or experimental condition.

Stage 5 — Data Classification

The analytical outputs are associated with their investigation IDs, experimental conditions, measurement channels, and source references.

This makes it possible to identify which result belongs to which experiment and which conditions apply.

Stage 6 — Visualization

The platform converts selected numerical information into charts, tables, and dashboard components.

Some time-series data are downsampled into compact browser-ready representations for visualization.

The downsampled data are intended for interactive display only and must not replace the full-resolution original files in scientific reanalysis.

Stage 7 — Scientific Quality Audit

The platform preserves important problems discovered during the inspection process.

These include missing calibration documents, ambiguous measurement channels, incomplete source files, conflicting identifiers, and incompatible experimental conditions.

The analytical output must make these limitations visible rather than silently correcting or ignoring them.

7. Comparative Analysis Between Investigations

The Comparison Workspace allows users to select and compare up to three investigations.

The comparison table organizes the following attributes:

  • Investigation title.
  • PSI identifier.
  • Evidence grade.
  • Gravity environment.
  • Experimental platform.
  • Hardware.
  • Material or fuel family.
  • Scientific topic.
  • Experimental variables.
  • Measurements.
  • Data status.
  • Data coverage.
  • Metadata completeness.
  • Known limitations.

The current implementation performs a preliminary comparison based on the gravity label and broad experimental family.

Even when both characteristics match, the interface warns users to verify oxygen concentration, pressure, gas composition, airflow, sample geometry, and measurement definitions before conducting quantitative comparisons.

When major differences exist, the comparison is labelled conceptual rather than directly comparable.

This is particularly important when evaluating the transferability of International Space Station experiments to lunar-habitat conditions.

8. Methodological and Data-Quality Auditing

The platform includes an explicit research-audit layer that identifies discrepancies and limitations in the available evidence.

The current implementation contains six major audit topics:

  1. PSI-107 investigation identifier conflict involving the DAFT / DAFT-2 inventory and the official SPICE record.
  2. SPICE publication-count discrepancy between 52 and 55 smoke-point results, alongside a separate 263-test-point count.
  3. Reversed ozone labels between PSI-142 Data IDs 1 and 2 in the CSV and Excel sources.
  4. Missing PSI-159 channel definitions and calibration information.
  5. Incomplete coverage of the uploaded experimental files.
  6. The distinction between ISS microgravity experiments and direct lunar partial-gravity experiments.

Each audit record includes a description of the problem and links to associated references where available.

The audit system ensures that unresolved research issues remain visible throughout the investigation, analysis, and comparison process.

9. AI-Assisted Scientific Information Retrieval

The research assistant is intended to help users navigate the curated scientific evidence.

Its role includes identifying relevant investigation records, retrieving associated scientific information, presenting relevant source references, and retaining important experimental limitations.

A user asking about solid-material flammability, for example, should be directed toward BASS-II and the relevant SoFIE investigations, whereas a question about aerosol properties should lead toward SAME/SAME-R and the relevant sensor research.

The evidence retrieval process should prioritize the available source records rather than relying only on general scientific knowledge.

Generated scientific explanations must remain distinguishable from directly measured experimental results.

The AI assistant must not invent unavailable values, assign unverified units, or claim that a research objective represents a completed experimental result.

10. Overall Analytical Contribution

The main analytical contribution of LFAEA is the integration of several research-information layers into a single structured environment.

These layers include:

  1. Literature summarization.
  2. Investigation classification.
  3. Experimental metadata organization.
  4. Descriptive numerical data analysis.
  5. Research prioritization.
  6. Comparative experimental analysis.
  7. Scientific data-quality auditing.
  8. Source-linked AI-assisted information retrieval.

By connecting these components, LFAEA provides a systematic method for exploring the relationship between combustion behavior, environmental conditions, material characteristics, smoke aerosol formation, and spacecraft fire-safety research.

The platform emphasizes traceability, reproducibility, experimental context, and scientific uncertainty.

Its central objective is not to generate unsupported universal conclusions, but to make the available experimental evidence easier to discover, interpret, and evaluate.
